cells.tense: You are here, reading the room and adjusting the mix as it happens.
cells.ask: In your next group conversation, offer one small blend of what two people just said, then stop and let the room take it or leave it.
cells.core: You can feel when the room needs more of one thing and less of another, and you move with that. Not by forcing a compromise, but by sensing what's missing and adding it. People find their own footing around that, and you stay easy in it because you're not steering anyone — you're noticing and shifting as you go.\n\nThat ease is the sign it's working. You hold several different views at once without flattening them, and what's actually happening stays in front of what you planned. The work now is to keep offering that blend, even when nobody notices where it came from. One small adjustment at a time, and the shared thing stays alive.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the mix alive by sensing what the room needs.
cells.verb: Sensing and blending what is in the room, keeping the mix alive
cells.place: In the chair where you decide what matters and what gets left out

cells.tense: You are already bracing for a conflict that has not arrived, smoothing it before anyone speaks.
cells.ask: Let one disagreement stand unresolved in the room for a full day. Don't fix it, don't name it, just let it be there.
cells.core: You're ahead of the room, calming things before they get said. You can see the friction coming and you get there first, softening edges, blending the rough parts. It looks like care. From inside, it's the only way you know to keep the flow going.\n\nBut the smoothing costs the room its real shape. When you blend too early, nobody gets to find out what they actually think. The direction you choose is harmony, and it's a direction you can't unchoose once you've made it. Letting one disagreement breathe gives the mix its real proportions back. The movement you want comes from feeling what's actually here, not from what you're afraid is coming.

cells.tense: You were scattered by every engagement, and you are still standing at a door you already walked through.
cells.ask: Choose one person and one thing you both care about, and ask them what they think before you decide anything about it.
cells.core: Every engagement pulls you somewhere else. You come in with one direction and leave with five, none of them yours. The center you used to find in a room doesn't hold anymore, and you keep looking for it in the next conversation, the next person, the next adjustment.\n\nThat's not a failure of will. It's that you're running on empty. Direction takes a kind of contact with yourself that you've lost touch with, and trying harder to choose just scatters you more. What pulls you back isn't more effort. It's one real exchange with someone where you feel recognized and recognize them, without either of you disappearing into the other. That contact is the ground you choose from.
cells.sheetLine: Scattered by everything, you can't find the center to choose from.

cells.tense: You are already shaping what the group values, and you describe it as if it were happening on its own.
cells.ask: Name one thing you did this week that set the tone for a group, and tell yourself plainly that you did it. Not that it happened.
cells.core: You're already blending, already directing the mix. You sense what matters to the people around you and you quietly make room for it, or shut it down. The adjustment runs whether or not anyone sees it, including you. But you describe it like something the room did to itself, not something you were doing.\n\nThat's the gap: the doing is yours, and you're not claiming it. You'll say 'that's just how it went,' when really you chose what got said and what got dropped. Naming one of those moments — just once, to yourself — isn't taking credit. It's the simplest way back to the work. The shared meaning only stays alive if someone admits they're keeping it.
cells.sheetLine: You're setting the tone and calling it just how it went.
